subtitle: How two machines prove who they are and agree on the keys that protect an IPsec tunnel.
summary: IKEv2 is the protocol IPsec peers use to authenticate each other and to agree on encryption keys and algorithms automatically. A four-message exchange sets up an IKE Security Association, which then creates and rekeys the Child SAs that actually protect IP traffic. It runs over UDP ports 500 and 4500 and includes built-in retransmission, cookie-based flood protection and NAT traversal. RFC 7296 is the Internet Standard (STD 79) version and replaces RFC 5996.

eli5.summary: Before two computers can pass secret notes, they need to agree on a secret code and make sure each is talking to the right friend. IKEv2 is the quick whispered meeting where they do that, and where they swap to a fresh code every so often.

questions: what is the difference between ike_sa_init and ike_auth
why does ikev2 use udp port 4500

tldr.problem: IPsec needs both ends to share algorithms and keys, and setting those up by hand does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: Two request/response exchanges (IKE_SA_INIT then IKE_AUTH) run a Diffie-Hellman key exchange, authenticate both peers and set up the first Child SA, and later exchanges create, rekey or delete SAs.
tldr.outcome: IPsec tunnels get fresh, mutually authenticated keys automatically, which is why IKEv2 is the standard key management protocol for IPsec VPNs.

today: IKEv2 is the key exchange protocol behind most IPsec VPNs. It is built into the IPsec stacks of major operating systems and VPN gateways, and open-source implementations such as strongSwan and Libreswan are widely used. Several later RFCs extend this one. RFC 7296 is updated by RFC 7427 (signature authentication), RFC 8247 (algorithm guidance) and RFC 9370 (multiple key exchanges), among others.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
IPsec protects IP packets with encryption and integrity checks, but both ends first have to agree on which algorithms and keys to use. Doing that by hand "does not scale well", as the RFC puts it. The Internet Key Exchange (IKE) is the protocol that sets up that shared state automatically. This document is IKE version 2.

IKE does two jobs at once. It mutually authenticates the two parties, and it creates an IKE Security Association (SA): a set of shared secrets and agreed algorithms. That IKE SA is then used to create Child SAs, the ESP or AH tunnels that carry the real traffic. Everything happens in request/response pairs called exchanges, and the requester is responsible for retransmitting if a reply never arrives.

RFC 7296 is not the first IKEv2 document. IKEv1 was spread across RFC 2409 and two companion documents, IKEv2 first appeared as RFC 4306, and RFC 5996 clarified it. RFC 7296 replaces RFC 5996 with minor revisions so that the protocol could advance to Internet Standard, and it is also published as STD 79.

IKE is the control channel, not the data channel. The packets that carry your traffic are protected by ESP or AH (see RFC 4303); IKE only negotiates and keys them.
sections.eli5: Two kids want to pass secret notes in class, but first they have to agree on a secret code and make sure each one is really talking to the right friend, not a stranger. IKE is the quick whispered meeting where they check each other's names, pick a code, and then pick a fresh code every so often.

sections.title: The Initial Exchanges
sections.content:
Every IKE conversation starts with two exchanges, four messages in the normal case. They are called IKE_SA_INIT and IKE_AUTH.

IKE_SA_INIT is sent in the clear. The initiator sends the cryptographic algorithms it supports (SAi1), its Diffie-Hellman value (KEi) and a nonce (Ni). The responder answers with its chosen suite (SAr1), its own Diffie-Hellman value (KEr) and its nonce (Nr), optionally with a certificate request. At this point both sides can compute SKEYSEED and every key derived from it.

IKE_AUTH is encrypted and integrity protected with those new keys. The initiator reveals its identity (IDi), proves it with an AUTH payload, and starts negotiating the first Child SA (SAi2 plus the traffic selectors TSi and TSr). The responder does the same with IDr, AUTH and SAr2. Because this happens inside encryption, identities are hidden from eavesdroppers.

The initiator sends its Diffie-Hellman value before it knows which group the responder prefers, so it must guess. If it guesses wrong, the responder replies with an INVALID_KE_PAYLOAD notification naming its chosen group, and the initiator retries with its full list of acceptable suites again.

If setting up the Child SA fails in IKE_AUTH (for example NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN or TS_UNACCEPTABLE), the IKE SA is still created. If authentication itself fails (AUTHENTICATION_FAILED), it is not.
sections.eli5: First you whisper in the hallway where anyone could listen: "here are the codes I know, and here is a number I made up." Both of you mix your numbers into a secret nobody else can figure out. Then you switch to that secret code to show your ID cards and agree on the code for your real conversation.

sections.title: Keys and Authentication
sections.content:
The Diffie-Hellman exchange in IKE_SA_INIT gives both sides a shared secret, g^ir, that an eavesdropper cannot compute. Each side then runs it through the negotiated pseudorandom function (prf) together with both nonces:

SKEYSEED = prf(Ni | Nr, g^ir)

From SKEYSEED, a longer function called prf+ stretches out seven keys, in this order: SK_d, SK_ai, SK_ar, SK_ei, SK_er, SK_pi, SK_pr. The two directions of traffic use different keys, so a message cannot be turned around and replayed back at its sender.

Authentication is separate from key agreement. Each side signs (or MACs with a shared secret) a block that starts with its own IKE_SA_INIT message, then appends the other side's nonce and a MAC of its own identity. The RFC calls it critical that each side sign the other side's nonce, which ties the signature to this exact exchange and prevents replay. Methods in this document are RSA digital signature, shared-key MAC and DSS digital signature.

For "legacy" user logins, an initiator may leave out the AUTH payload and use EAP, the Extensible Authentication Protocol (RFC 3748). EAP is only allowed together with a public-key-signature authentication of the responder, and it adds extra IKE_AUTH exchanges (message IDs 2, 3 and so on).
sections.eli5: Each of you has a secret number and you do a clever trick that lets you both end up with the same shared secret without ever saying it out loud. From that one secret you make a whole key ring: some keys to lock messages, some to prove nobody changed them, and different ones for each direction. Then each of you proves who you are by signing a note that includes the other person's random number.

sections.title: Message Format
sections.content:
One IKE message travels in one UDP datagram, on UDP port 500 or 4500. It starts with a fixed 28-byte IKE header followed by a chain of payloads. The header carries two 8-byte SPIs (the initiator's and the responder's), the Next Payload type, a major and minor version (both 4 bits, here 2 and 0), the Exchange Type, a flags byte, a 32-bit Message ID and a 32-bit total Length.

The exchange types are 34 (IKE_SA_INIT), 35 (IKE_AUTH), 36 (CREATE_CHILD_SA) and 37 (INFORMATIONAL). In the flags byte, the I bit is set by whoever originally started the IKE SA, and the R bit is set on every response. Because the sender's own SPI is in every packet, receivers use the I bit to tell which of the two SPIs is theirs.

Each payload begins with a 4-byte generic header: Next Payload (1 byte), a Critical bit plus seven reserved bits, and a 2-byte Payload Length. A Next Payload of 0 ends the chain. Payload types run from 33 (SA) through 48 (EAP), including KE 34, IDi 35, IDr 36, CERT 37, CERTREQ 38, AUTH 39, Nonce 40, Notify 41, Delete 42, Vendor ID 43, TSi 44, TSr 45, Encrypted (SK) 46 and Configuration 47.

After the IKE_SA_INIT exchange the payloads are wrapped in a single Encrypted payload, which must be last in the message. It holds an IV, the encrypted payloads, padding, a pad length and an integrity checksum.

On UDP port 4500, every IKE message is preceded by four zero bytes. Those four bytes are not part of the IKE message and are not counted in its Length.
sections.eli5: Every IKE message is like a letter with a standard envelope on the outside that says who it is from, what kind of letter it is, and how long it is. Inside are little labelled cards, one after another, and each card says what kind of card comes next. After the first two letters, all the cards go into a locked box.

sections.title: Negotiating Algorithms
sections.content:
The SA payload is how two peers agree on algorithms. It is built as a nested structure: an SA payload holds one or more proposals, each proposal names one protocol (IKE = 1, AH = 2, ESP = 3), and each proposal holds transforms. Proposals are numbered from 1 and listed from most to least preferred. The responder picks one and echoes back the matching proposal number.

Transforms have a type: encryption (1), pseudorandom function (2), integrity (3), Diffie-Hellman group (4) and extended sequence numbers (5). The rule for combining them is simple. Several transforms of the same type in a proposal mean OR. Transforms of different types mean AND. So proposing "AES or 3DES, with SHA-1" fits in one proposal, but "3DES with MD5, or IDEA with SHA" needs two proposals.

A transform may carry attributes, mainly a key length, so offering AES-128, AES-192 and AES-256 takes three transforms with one Key Length attribute each. Combined-mode ciphers that do their own integrity checking go in a separate proposal from ordinary ciphers.

The IKE_AUTH exchange carries no KE or nonce payloads, so its SA payload cannot meaningfully include a Diffie-Hellman transform. Extra Diffie-Hellman for a Child SA is done in CREATE_CHILD_SA.

OR within a type
Two ENCR transforms in a proposal means "either one".
AND across types
An ENCR plus an INTEG transform means "one of each".
sections.eli5: It is like ordering at a restaurant. You say "I would like pasta or pizza, and juice or milk." If you want pasta with juice, or pizza with milk, but nothing else, you have to give two separate orders. The waiter picks one choice from each group that the kitchen can make and repeats it back.

sections.title: Later Exchanges and Rekeying
sections.content:
Once the initial exchanges finish, either side can start two more kinds of exchange, both encrypted.

CREATE_CHILD_SA creates a new Child SA, or rekeys an existing Child SA or the IKE SA itself. The request carries SA offers and a nonce, optionally a KE payload for a fresh Diffie-Hellman exchange (stronger forward secrecy), and traffic selectors when making Child SAs. A responder may refuse with NO_ADDITIONAL_SAS.

INFORMATIONAL carries Notify, Delete and Configuration payloads: error reports, requests to delete an SA, and so on. A request with no payloads other than the empty Encrypted wrapper is the standard liveness check, and the peer must answer, even if only with an empty response.

Traffic selectors say which packets belong in a Child SA. Each selector is an address range, a port range and an IP protocol. TSi describes the initiator side and TSr the responder side. The responder may narrow the proposal to a subset.

SAs are never extended, only replaced. To rekey, create a new equivalent SA first and then delete the old one. Child SA keys come from SK_d, the new nonces and an optional new Diffie-Hellman value. If both ends rekey at the same moment you get redundant SAs, so the RFC says rekey timing SHOULD be jittered.

Rekeying with CREATE_CHILD_SA but no new Diffie-Hellman exchange leaves all the SAs exposed if a single key is ever broken. The RFC tells implementers to limit how many such rekeys happen between Diffie-Hellman exponentiations, but does not prescribe a limit.
sections.eli5: After you are chatting, either of you can say "let's get a second secret code for a new game" or "let's change our codes, the old ones are getting stale." You make the new code first, start using it, and only then throw away the old one. Or you can just tap your friend on the shoulder to ask "still there?" and they have to tap back.

sections.title: Reliability, Cookies and NAT
sections.content:
IKE runs on unreliable UDP, so reliability is built in. Messages come in pairs, and the initiator retransmits the request until it gets the response. A retransmission must be bitwise identical to the original, from the IKE header onward, and uses the same Message ID. The Message ID is 0 for IKE_SA_INIT and increases with each later exchange. A responder never retransmits unprompted, and may forget old responses after several minutes. Normally one request is outstanding at a time; the SET_WINDOW_SIZE notification lets a peer allow more.

IKE_SA_INIT is a target for floods of forged requests. A responder that sees many half-open IKE SAs can reply with a COOKIE notification of 1 to 64 bytes and keep no state. The initiator must repeat its request with the cookie as the first payload. The RFC suggests a cookie made from a secret version number plus a hash of Ni, the initiator's IP and SPI, and a secret that is changed often.

NATs break IPsec in several ways, so IKEv2 supports NAT traversal. Each side sends NAT_DETECTION_SOURCE_IP and NAT_DETECTION_DESTINATION_IP notifications carrying SHA-1 hashes of SPIs, addresses and ports. A mismatch reveals a NAT in the path. Both sides then move to UDP port 4500 and wrap ESP in UDP. IKE packets MUST be accepted from any source port, because NATs rewrite them.

All implementations must handle IKE messages up to 1280 octets and SHOULD handle up to 3000. IKE has no fragmentation of its own.
sections.eli5: If a letter gets lost in the mail, the sender keeps sending the same letter until a reply comes back. To stop troublemakers from flooding the office with fake letters, the receptionist can say "write back and include this ticket number" before opening a file on you. And if a doorman at your building keeps changing your return address, you both agree to meet at a special door that he leaves alone.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
IKE is built to give little away to strangers, but some disclosure is unavoidable. The initiator must identify itself first, so it can learn that the responder speaks IKE and which algorithms it supports. A fake responder can probe an initiator for its identity, and via CERTREQ payloads for which certificates it will accept. With EAP the order reverses for part of the exchange, so an attacker can probe the responder.

Because IKE_SA_INIT and IKE_AUTH happen before the initiator is authenticated, implementations must be robust against attacks from unauthenticated peers, especially denial of service. This is flagged as a particular worry for EAP, which allows an unbounded number of messages.

Randomness matters a great deal. Nonces and Diffie-Hellman exponents must come from a strong random source, and exponents should be erased from memory after use. A PRF whose output is under 128 bits MUST NOT be used, and implementations MUST NOT negotiate NONE as the IKE integrity algorithm or ENCR_NULL as the IKE encryption algorithm.

With pre-shared keys, the secret should have as much randomness as the strongest key being negotiated. Deriving a key from a password or name is not secure and is open to dictionary attacks. The NAT detection hashes can also leak a hidden internal IPv4 address to an attacker who is willing to try all possibilities.

The Diffie-Hellman group discussion in this RFC dates from 2014. For current algorithm requirements and guidance, see RFC 8247.
sections.eli5: Even a secret handshake gives a few things away: whoever goes first has to say who they are. So the rules say to use really random numbers, never use a guessable password as your secret, and always have a plan for people who try to flood the door with fake knocks.

fields.name: Initiator's SPI
fields.desc: Chosen by the original initiator to identify one IKE SA. Must not be zero.

fields.name: Responder's SPI
fields.desc: Chosen by the responder. Must be zero in the first message of an initial exchange, including a repeat that carries a cookie.

fields.name: Next Payload
fields.desc: Type of the payload that follows the header (0 = none).

fields.name: MjVer
fields.desc: Major version. Must be set to 2.

fields.name: MnVer
fields.desc: Minor version. Must be set to 0 and is ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Bits X X R V I X X X. R (Response) is set on every response. I (Initiator) is set by the original initiator of the IKE SA. V is cleared when sending and ignored on receipt. X bits are cleared when sending.

fields.name: Message ID
fields.desc: Matches requests to responses and detects retransmissions. Zero in IKE_SA_INIT messages, then incremented for each exchange.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length in octets of the whole message, header plus payloads.

fields.name: Next Payload
fields.desc: Type of the next payload in the message. 0 if this is the last. In an Encrypted payload it names the first payload inside.

fields.name: C
fields.desc: Critical bit. Set to one if the recipient should reject the whole message when it does not understand this payload type. Zero for all payload types defined in this document.

fields.name: RESERVED
fields.desc: Sent as zero, ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Payload Length
fields.desc: Length in octets of this payload, including this generic header.
